item.title: Adapting the DfR Browser
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
item.description:
At the core of the dissertation is a 250 topic model of the periodical literature of the denomination. As I discuss throughout the dissertation, topic modeling is a form of unsupervised machine learning that enables the exploration of a corpus of literature based on the co-occurrence of words, clustered into units called “topics.” While for the computer, the topics represent the likelihood of word occurrences in different contexts, for the human reader the topic can be used to track different themes or discourses within a corpus. And although the model tends to be unstable, in that as a probabilistic representation of the words in a corpus, it will represent the text differently each time the algorithm is run, it provides a useful abstraction of a corpus of literature, a possible interpretation that highlights different features of the collection of texts.

I created the model using a number of computational tools, including the Python library Gensim and MALLET through the command line interface. Topic models are informationally dense representations of a corpus, and as such are most useful for corpus exploration when coupled with some sort of interactive visualization. Such visualizations enable the reader to focus on in particular aspects of the corpus, pointing to further areas for investigation.

For this project, I have used the DfR Browser, created by Andrew Goldstone. While not the only topic model interface available, the DfR Browser has a number of advantages. First, structurally the browser is a static, single-site website, which reduces the complexity of hosting and archiving the work. Second, the browser provides a number of useful interfaces into the topic model data, enabling the reader to see from the level of the overall model and corpus to the level of individual words. Third, the methods used by Goldstone to calculate topic weights over time are similar to those I use throughout the rest of the dissertation, computing the percentage of total tokens each year assigned to each topic. This consistency provides a consistent representation of the topics between the visualizations within the dissertation and the browser, which is vital when moving from the model to interpretation.

To aid in the use of the browser, I provide an overview of the different “view” available within the model browser to help orient the reader and clarify the ways I anticipate the model being used.1 These views are the full model view, the topic level view, the document level view, and the word level view. Each provides a different window onto the tokens within the corpus of Seventh-day Adventist periodical literature and can be used to explore different aspects of the model and of the literature over time.

The Model View

The landing page of the model browser enables the user to view the overall structure of the topic model and provides four different views of all of the topics. The “Grid” view shows all the topics as circles, with the boundary widths indicating overall prominence, while the “Scaled” view (currently not functional) varies the size of the circles according to the prominence of the topic. The “List” view is one of the most productive if interested in change over time. In this view, the topics are listed alphabetically with a miniaturized chart of prevalence over time as well as overall proportion in the corpus, and can be sorted along any of these columns. And finally, the “Stacked” view provides visualization of all of the topics, with band width corresponding to percentage of total words, or word counts, depending on the user selection.

The model level view provides the user insight into the overall structure of the topic model. In these views, we can see that there is a large number of topics for the corpus, with both more generalized and focused topics. Because of the amount of data generated with this many topics, documents, and words, the overall view provides suggestions of places for further inquiry, but offers few clear suggestions of patterns in the overall corpus.

The Topic View

The topic level views allows the user to explore each topic individually in terms of the words that are most prominently associated with the topic, as well as the documents where the highest percentage of tokens is assigned to the topic. Additionally, when a user selects a year in the graph of “conditional probability of words in topic,” the top documents update to reveal the top occurrences of the topic in that year, rather than across all documents. These interface features enable the user to explore which areas of the corpus are most strongly associated with a particular topic.

This information, combined with the graph of topics over time, helps illuminate the patterns in language use identified by the model. I used this information in assigning interpretive labels to the topic, reading the context from the top documents as well as exploring particular years, both with low and high overall prevalence, in order to further refine my understanding of the topics. While the perceived accuracy of the topic assignment decreases with the number of tokens assigned to the topic, for the high prevalence assignments, the view helps illuminate the patterns of language and content captured in the model.2

The Document View

The document level view provides a close view of how the topic modeling algorithm labeled the words within each document, showing each identified topic and the number and percentage of words associated with it. This breakdown of topic assignments provides something of a summary of the content of the document, indicating which general themes or discourses the document is likely engaged with. The view also provides some initial indication as to which topics might be linked to one another.

The document level view can also be used to begin to evaluate the performance of the topic modeling algorithm. In the case of the document linked here, the long list of identified topics, many with only one word associated with it, suggests that the topic model could be further refined by encouraging fewer topic assignments within documents, an aspect controlled through the alpha hyperparameter of the modeling algorithm.3 Despite this weakness, the top three topics assigned to the document provide a good indication of the content of the document, which is a personal testimonial of conversion experience of one of the students at the school.

The Word View

The word level view has two main interfaces: the first shows all of the words that appear in the top 20 for topics and the second shows the topics in which individual words appear. These two interfaces provide insight into the overall language use within the full set of documents, as well as the ways the topic model treated the individual words from the texts. The full list shows the most prominent words that appear in the corpus, providing an unusual but interesting summary of the language of the denomination. The topic view for individual words reveals how words have been grouped with the algorithm, together with the interpretive label I assigned to that cluster of language. This interface provides another way to engage the corpus, working from key words of interest through the associated topics to the documents.

Conclusion

The DfR Browser is well designed to provide users with both a high-level view of a topic model, as well as the more detailed information needed for evaluating the strengths of the model and using the model to identify documents related to a subject of inquiry. The four views of the browser let the users move back and forth between these different views of the corpus and its language, a key feature for putting the model to interpretive work. While not the only topic model browser under development, this approach has significant advantages for research work in humanities contexts, as it grounds the interface in teh documents, rather than the model itself. Additionally, the technical load of the browser is light, simplifying the processes involved in presenting and archiving the model interface.

My dissertation project has also brought to light some additional features that would enhance the browser for model exploration and interpretation. The default set up for the browser enables exploration of the topic model, but not further manipulation of the model data. While the algorithm currently clusters topics based on time, enabling further grouping of documents and topics based on other metadata variables at the level of the user interface would enable additional exploration into the ways particular topics, or discourses are distributed by things such as publication type or geographic region.4 Additional, the inclusion of the document text within the document view, with the topic assignment of the words indicated in some way, would provide further useful information on how the model has characterized the language of the document. Finally, a reporting mechanism that would enable returning a collections of documents that fit a particularly set of parameters would expand the usefulness of the browser from the exploration of a model to leveraging the clustering work of the algorithm to identify related documents on a given topic.

A number of these changes push the interface beyond what can be achieved within a static site, as the memory load on the browser becomes difficult to support. As such, it is also worth considering an adaptation of the browser that relies on a database for serving the corpus and model data. This modification would remove some of the advantages of the static-site approach, but would make the browser a more robust tool for research.

Leveraging a topic model for historical research is a multifaceted problem, extending from the work of the selection and preparation of a set of literature to the interfaces for interpreting and utilizing the resulting data. While experimental work in the digital humanities has focused largely on the process of running the topic modeling algorithm on a set of documents, there is significant research to be done on the pre-processing and post-processing steps that make the running of the algorithm possible and legible. As both of these greatly shape the results of the computational analysis and its usefulness in historical research, they are vital areas for further scholarly attention from scholars working at the intersection of computation and the humanities.

item.title: Anticipating the End of Time
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
item.description:
“We are living in the closing scenes of this earth’s history. Prophecy is fast fulfilling. The hours of probation are fast passing. We have no time – not a moment – to lose.”
Ellen White. Testimonies for the Church, Volume 8, 19041

Early Seventh-day Adventists were a people between times. Born out of the belief that William Miller had correctly identified 1844 as the year revealed in the books of Daniel and Revelations, this group of Protestant Christians understood themselves to be living in the last days, preparing for the rapidly approaching “second advent” of Jesus. Millennial expectation, however, is a difficult state to maintain. Although Seventh-day Adventists determined early on that predicting new dates for the second coming was no longer viable, at various period throughout their early history they understood themselves to be at the brink of the second coming. As the second coming continued to be delayed, their interpretations of the events since 1844 shifted, as did the emphasis they placed on different religious beliefs and practices. As a result, their theology and religious culture was shaped by “Jesus’ nonappearance rather than his imminent reappearance,” as the most productive periods of development tended to occur in efforts to explain the why of the continuation of normal time.2

The Seventh-day Adventist experience of time shaped the development of their religious culture in ways that reflected the general renegotiation of time that took place during the nineteenth century, but also challenged them. They held to what they understood to be biblical organizations of time as the surrounding culture increasingly embraced the authority of mechanical standards for time; they rejected the long time scales required by evolution in favor of the shorter time frame of a literal understanding of the creation story; they interpreted the technological advances and political changes of the time within a framework of decline prior to the second coming, rather than as evidence of progress. As a result, while the nineteenth century was generally marked by a “masculine” culture that privileged progress, history, and technological control over nature - from which women were largely excluded - the culture of Seventh-day Adventism offered an instructive alternative. While still shaped by religiously-informed patriarchal ideas of authority, their concurrent embrace of “natural” (or “Biblical”) organizations of time, as well as of the physical health and salvation of embodied humans as the crux of the Christian message, created space for more “feminine” cultural features, such as an emphasis on community over personal gain and the importance of human development as part of Christian discipline, including parenting as well as care for neighbors.3 As a result, while explicit support for women in leadership positions varied over the early years of denomination, on the whole the religious life encouraged by the denomination provided space for and recognition of the contribution of women to the religious and cultural goals of the denomination, particularly while it was guided by the leadership of Ellen G. White.

The development of this unique religious culture was shaped in large part by the shifting sense of urgency regarding the end of times. While formal predictions of the second coming were relatively rare and not encouraged after 1844, events both internal and external to the denomination sparked periods of heightened end-times expectation during the first seventy years of their history. Using the 250 topic model of the periodical literature of the denomination, I identify and discuss the cycles of expectation and explanation that mark the early development of the Seventh-day Adventist denomination. Using topics that capture Seventh-day Adventist language about end times as indicators of high periods of expectation, I argue that the religious group experienced four major cycles of expectation and adjustment between 1849 and 1920. In each cycle, the markers of the anticipated second coming shift and in the wake of anticipation, new emphases emerged that shifted the focus of the denomination increasingly outward.

Time and the Religious Culture of Seventh-day Adventism

The early Seventh-day Adventist church provides a useful entry point to the relationship between “time” and culture, as the denomination developed during a period of reorganization of previously standard conceptions of time while also organizing itself around a particular set of beliefs regarding time: that time was nearly at an end and that salvation was linked to a proper ordering of time. Although rarely thought about directly, time is an unstable feature of human experience and one that is profoundly shaped by the conceptual and narrative frameworks through which one interprets the world. While debates regarding the organization of time were not unique to the nineteenth century, the century was one of particular upheaval in terms of standard assumptions about time, as understandings of history, of progress, of government, and of Christianity all underwent significant revision in the face of political revolutions and advances in science and technology. Older assumptions of time as cyclical, already under stress from the changes of the Reformation and the Enlightenment, gave way to a sense of time as linear, as unique and irreversible. Under a linear framework, the dramatic political reorganizations could be understood as unique, and as representing progress from the older model of the divine rights of kings to all men being created equal, capable of and entitled to self-government. History itself, in this context, became the work of identifying and articulating that progress (through narrative).4 Within the realm of religion, standard practices and assumptions of Christianity, which had historically contained both cyclical and linear patterns of time, shifted to privileging the linear. Emphasizing Genesis to Revelations as a describing the start and end of historical time, nineteenth-century Christians, particularly Protestants, were primed to interpret their lives and world events as part of a divine historical drama moving quickly toward its completion.5 For many, this embrace of linear time also corresponded with an embrace of a narrative of progress, couched in religious terms as hope in human perfectibility or of the potential for ushering in the millennium through conversions.

The development of technology and science also contributed to significant changes in the conception and experience of time during the nineteenth century. Central to these shifts was the growing prevalence of and reliance on clocks as devices that not just reflected time, but were the source and arbiter of time itself. Previous generations conceptualized time as determined first by the sun, and then captured by the clock, and as a result, time was understood to vary by locality, depending on ones position relative to the earth’s orbit. This system worked well enough when most people remained within a relatively geographic space. The development and spread of the railroad, however, introduced new logistical challenges to the keeping of time, enabling persons and goods to move long distances quickly and in doing so moving through multiple local times. The slow adoption to standardized time and the current timezone configurations was part of a reshaping of notions of time, from a natural feature of the world marked by the sun and other regular rhythms of agriculture and human bodies to an abstract, mechanical reality set by some authority and disconnected from the variations of the physical world.6

While technology in the form of clocks and railroads reshaped the daily experience of time, the broader understanding of historical time, of the extent of the past, was also coming under revision with advances in science, particularly with the development of the publication of Darwin’s On the Origin of Species. Previously the sense of cosmic time was guided by the Genesis story, where the world came into being through divine command approximately four thousand years ago and established for the dominion of “man.” Darwin’s theory of evolution, as well as other scientific developments in areas such as geology, challenged that religiously derived sense of time. These theories forwarded a long and largely impersonal historical account, one in which human beings appeared only briefly and which seemed governed more by chance than by the careful plan of a benevolent god. As a means of confronting this more chaotic picture of time, many embraced a historical narrative of progress, with evolutionary processes leading toward the improvement and gradual perfection of human beings and society.7

Making sense of time and creating narratives that would give meaning to experience in the face of such upheaval presented a major challenge for nineteenth-century authors. One strategy was to turn to gender as a means of creating and clarifying the new relationship with history, with technology, and with religion. For many American (male) intellectuals, gaining mastery over the new conceptions of time frequently entailed reinforcing binaries, such as those between men and women, between races, and between cultures. As a result, literary authors and others relied on tropes that associated “the male with history and the female with ahistoricity; the male with intellectual acuity and the female with mental deficiency, based on Darwinian presumptions; the male with progressive civilization and the female with stultifying primitivism; or the male with Christianity and the female with paganism.”8 While the social and political world was organized along a vision of linear and progressive time, as determined by the “objective” arbiters of science and technology, “women’s time” was different and was composed of “the cyclical time that conforms to nature through gestation, regularity, and biological rhythms, and the monumental time that evokes infinity through its affiliation with myth, mysticism, and the cosmos.”9 Bound to monthly cycles as well as the cycles of childbearing, women were presented as a foil against which masculine mastery over time was brought into being. In fact, all those who embraced other organizations of time found themselves outside of the cultural mainstream and its power structures, including the early Seventh-day Adventists.

For Seventh-day Adventists, these shifting temporal markers shaped the religious culture of the denomination, as members worked to articulate their own understandings of time, one that rooted time in the natural world as understood through a literal interpretation of the Bible, while also enabling believers to inhabit the increasingly mechanistic world of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Their conception of time developed along a number of different lines. One of the earliest elements of Seventh-day Adventist time can be seen in the debates surrounding Sabbath-keeping, and their linking of Saturday Sabbath to the natural order of time established in creation. While inhabiting standard time, they maintained older cyclical rhythms around their religious practice, using the sun, rather than the clock, to mark the start of the Sabbath on Friday evening.10 Similarly, they rejected evolutionary science and the concurrent reorganization of historical time, insisting instead on the creation narrative understood in terms of literal days and a temporally short period of the world.11 Uniting these approaches, their orientation toward standard time and toward historical time was informed by their beliefs around the second coming and eschatological time, and their belief that history was moving rapidly toward its completion, marked not by gradual progress but by the persecution of Seventh-day Adventists and their salvation through the Second Coming of Jesus.

Through their embrace of different temporal paradigms, early Seventh-day Adventists created a religious culture that was in tension with that of other nineteenth-century Protestants, one where alternative orderings of gender were able to thrive at various times in their development. From a weekly rhythm guided by the natural “time” of the sun to a historical and cosmic narrative focused not on progress but on disruption leading up to the rapidly approaching completion of history. While always in conversation with the progress-oriented, evolutionary, and standardized time of their surrounding culture, the distinctive temporal imaginary of the Seventh-day Adventists created space for the continued leadership of Ellen White, and for a sharing of the labor of preparing for the second coming, both within the context of the home and family and in the context of the missions.

Maintaining an alternative temporal imaginary and cultural framework is no small task. As the nineteenth century progressed, arguments over the organization of time also heightened as seen in a variety of social issues, from aggitation for Sunday observance laws to public debates over evolution in the Scopes Trial. For Seventh-day Adventists, such challenges to their sense of time were understood in religious terms, particularly in terms of eschatology or the overarching narrative of salvation and the end of time. In fact, it seems likely that denominational leaders ongoing commitment to that foundational temporal arrangement - the impending end of the world - helped reinforce their alternative sense of lived and historical time.

However, expectation of the end of the world is difficult to sustain over long periods of time. In his Foreword to William McLoughlin’s Revivals, Awakening and Reform, Martin Marty notes that “Individuals do not ordinarily live their lives at a single pitch of intensity. Periods of high drama are interspersed among longer periods of mild boredom. After times of vitality come stretches of exhaustion. As with individuals, so with cultures.”12 End-times expectation, that sense of living at the monumental close of history, is one such period of high drama and one that has reoccurred at various points in Christian history, and is particularly entwined with the history of Protestantism in the United States.13 For Seventh-day Adventists, who trace their roots to one of the more notable surges in end-times expectation at the close of the Second Great Awakening, time and end times expectation is core to their religious culture. However, just as with their contemporaries, the pitch of expectation varied over their history. As a result, rather than a consistent awareness of and focus on the second coming, we would expect to see a cyclical pattern around periods when the second coming seemed, for one reason or another, particularly likely.

Such cycles also contribute to instability in other cultural aspects of the denomination, including ideas about gender and the roles available to women within the denominational structure. With increased attention to questions of gender, race, and class, scholars who examine patterns across multiple revivals have drawn attention to the ways women and members of other marginalized groups feature prominently during periods of upheaval or revival. Such analysis has been done using the frameworks of theorists such as Mary Douglas, Victor Turner, and Max Weber, parsing revival periods as moments of disruption in social norms and hierarchies, where members reject or challenge existing rituals until a new equilibrium is achieved and order is re-established.14 These frameworks help explain periods of unusually expansive behavior within religious and cultural groups, as well as the more subtle but lasting cultural shifts that revival moments leave in their wake.15

For early Seventh-day Adventism, the standard historical narrative has been one of slow accommodation to the surrounding culture, where Seventh-day Adventism progressed from a group at the edges of the Millerite movement to an established denomination, and one that was increasingly inscribing a gendered hierarchy based on “separate spheres” and female domesticity by the 1920s.16 These general patterns of accommodation and secularization - in the sense of becoming “like the world” - help explain the overall structural shifts in the Seventh-day Adventist theology and religious culture, but also obscure the ways that culture was negotiated at multiple point along the way. While Vance and Butler convincingly argue that trajectory of the Seventh-day Adventist denomination has historically been toward accommodation to prevailing cultural norms and toward increased affiliation with the traditional Protestant denomination, the early years of the sect indicate that this progression was complex and contested. As Vance notes with regard to Ellen White’s positions on female leadership in the denomination, “the seeming contradictions of White’s admonitions, life, and advice are not easily reconciled.”17

By looking at the shorter timescale of the first seventy years of the denomination, those when the church was lead by Ellen White, we can begin to add another layer to our picture of nineteenth-century revivalism and the processes by which distinctive religious cultures develop, in this case around the key issue of time. While the overall trajectory of Seventh-day Adventism has been toward increased connection and accommodation to rest of American Protestantism, albeit with a heightened awareness of the end of time, the distinctive elements of the denomination’s culture, including the ongoing leadership of Ellen White and the promotion of alternative forms of masculinity and femininity, point to additional factors shaping that development. If, rather than a linear decline from the intensity of 1844, we assume a cyclical pattern to the Seventh-day Adventist sense of time, with the second coming seeming more or less imminent at different points through out their history, we can begin to explore the relationship between those periods of intensity and “boredom” with shifts in the locus on salvation and the ways the work to bring salvation about were gendered.

To find and explore these cycles requires examining the literature of the denomination at distance, an angle made possible through the use of computational text analysis. In this study, I use topic modeling to explore the seeming contradictions and changing emphases of the first seventy years of the denomination in light of two, I argue, related influences on Adventist thought: belief in the second coming and constructions of gender and ideas regarding female authority. First, I proceed from the assumption that early Adventist writers truly did believe themselves to be living at the edge of the second coming, that their experiences of the world were shaped by reference to a shortened temporal horizon or temporal imaginary. While their sense of time lengthens and the theological particulars change over time, the development of Seventh-day Adventism was critically shaped by their commitment to the Jesus’ imminent second coming, a belief felt at different times more acutely that others. Second, I posit that those periods of heightened expectation trigger periods of disruption, or “religious anti-ritualism,” when power structures and religious commitments are re-examined, both in the midst of expectation and in the realignments that follow as time persists.18 Through these cycles, as I show through this case study, the “world” to be reached with the Adventist message slowly widens and the understanding of that message expands. Due in large part to Ellen White’s continued leadership within the movement and through the upheavals brought on by periods of end-times expectation, at each turn and reformulation of the Adventist message, the religious life is gendered for both men and women in ways at odds with prevailing cultural norms. While these role are also circumscribed and influenced by broader cultural constructions, the result is a religious culture where women are consistently central to the work of salvation, and the overall culture, while patriarchal, also contains markable “feminine” characteristics.

Methodology

One of the ongoing challenges for scholarship that brings together methods from multiple disciplines is articulating how the information derived through methods typically foreign to humanities practice meaningfully contributes to the process of meaning-making. As argued by Tanya Clement, the linking of theory and methods is crucial to the process of situating the intellectual work of interdisciplinary scholarship.19 As part of bridging that gap, here I outline my interpretive strategy for moving from the topic model, a statistical representation of language patterns, to an argument for overall patterns in the denominational corpus.20 The full model, which you can engage via the model browser, parses the language of the denomination into 250 clusters of words that tend to co-occur on the pages of the periodicals.

Topic modeling, as I discuss in the project overview, is a form of computational analysis that has been used in humanities context for descriptions of a collection of documents and for document discovery, but of which are fewer clear examples of use in historical analysis. This is, in part, because while tools like MALLET and Gensim make it easy to apply the algorithm to a set of texts, doing so in a way that generates reasonable and reliable results is more difficult. This project sets out to use a topic model of the denomination’s periodical literature, following the suggestion of Sharon Block and David Newman’s topic model explorations of the Pennsylvania Gazette, to highlight “topic trends over time and at different resolutions” and for gaining insight on “entire publications.”21 With this approach, I am focusing on using the model to gain a broad pictures of the patterns across the texts and to identify those texts that can shed light on different aspects of the developing culture of the denomination.

The modeling algorithm returns a topic identifier for each word in the documents, an account of the most prevalent words in each topic, and a report of the prevalence of each topic in the documents of the corpus, but is agnostic as to what those topics “mean.” Standard practice is to use a topic label to summarize the language that a topic has grouped together, either by assigning it automatically from the most prevalent words in the topic or through manually assigning topic names.22 Because the language used by Seventh-day Adventist authors tends to be abstract and formulaic, methods for automatic labeling that work well in the context of scientific articles or Wikipedia proved less than informative. As a result, I relied on a human authored approach for identifying and labeling the topics.

Labeling the topics represents significant interpretive work based on close readings of the texts and the topic words. To mitigate the risk of reading too much into individual combinations of words clustered by the modeling algorithm, for each topic I read the ten to fifteen documents with the highest concentration of words assigned to that topic, and used that contextual information, together with the words of the topic, to construct the label. This method of close reading the topic results provided a more nuanced view of the pattern of word use the model had detected and helped me parse instances where similar words in the topic captured very different sets of documents. For example, topic 6 shares similar language with the “prophecy” topics that I discuss in the next section, such as the high prevalence of “daniel” and “babylon.” However, in reading the documents associated with the topic, it was apparent that the words captured by this topic were most often found in pages that contained Old Testament stories, particularly those from the historical and prophetic books such as Daniel in the Lion’s Den and the story of Esther.

Through the process of labeling the generated topics, I as the reader and interpreter bridged the gap between the model of the denominations literature created using a statistical algorithm and the models of literature created through traditional close-reading techniques. Working with set of text too large for me to read thoroughly and establish the categories of which on my own, I use the model to separate the texts into groups based on language use, use close reading of a select number of documents to understand the themes that the topic model has captured, and then use the model to get a sense of how that theme is present in the documents I have not read.

In addition, in order to more easily facilitate grouping related topics together, I created a controlled vocabulary of [x] terms. The vocabulary works to capture the major topics of the periodical literature, as separated by the topic model and identified through my evaluation, and forms the first part of the topic label. The second part of the label provides a more detailed description of the type of content within that general category. I designed this labeling scheme in order to facilitate the research goals of the project. At 250 topics, the model of the literature strikes a compromise between being generalized and being detailed. As a result, there is some overlap in topics. This provides the advantage of nuance and increases the opportunity to see shifts in language over time. However, it also makes the model more difficult to read and understand, as the fragmentation of theme over multiple topics makes is difficult to grasp broader trends. By using the labels to group topics back together, I am able to add yet another lens through which to view the corpus literature.

The labels enable readers navigate the model and provide the foundation for the work that follows in which I trace the broader picture of the prevalence of particular subjects at different times. By moving back and forth between close readings of the text and the more abstract and distant reading of the model, the reader can begin to understand and explore the overall patterns in the literature and use those patterns to identify areas for closer analysis.

Identifying Expectation

In order to capture periods when Seventh-day Adventist writers and readers were focused more than usual on the second coming, I identified and traced four interrelated themes that capture the language denominational members used when speaking of the second coming and the end of time. The first theme highlights more formal explications of the key prophetic texts of Daniel and Revelations, where authors unpacked for the readers the meaning of the various figures and numbers in the biblical passages. The second contains descriptions of the second coming, where adventist writers worked to explain the events they anticipated as part of the second coming and to encourage believers to strive for the goal of heaven. The third is the parsing current and historical events in terms of their fulfillment of prophecy, or analyzing the “signs of the times.” The forth theme captures the SDA’s concern with the union of civic and religious authority. United by the idea that “Prophecy is history in advance,”23 in these themes Seventh-day Adventist authors and readers sought to understand where they stood in the temporal landscape, to verify their understanding of 1844 and their particular role in the unfolding of God’s plan, and to explain the events of the day in light of the larger trajectory of God’s plan.

In selecting these topics and organizing them into these four themes, I am offering an interpretation of the particular corpus, and Seventh-day Adventist literature in general, but also attempting to work with the strengths and limitations of the topic modeling algorithm. Topic modeling as a probabilistic algorithm, meaning that depending on where one starts, the algorithm can produce different results when run multiple times on the same corpus and even with the same parameters.24 As a result, individual words assigned to topic A in one model can be assigned to a very different topic M in another. As a result, the individual words say less than one might hope about the clustering of tokens and documents identified by the algorithm. As I discuss in the methodology, I have attempted to account for this in creating the topic labels by relying not only on the words assigned to the topic but by reading the documents where those words were drawn from. This second process of organizing topics into themes provides a second strategy for balancing the probabilistic aspect of topic modeling. When patterns repeat over a range of topics that are predominant in similar types of documents, the results are both clearer and more reliable. [plan: the effects of these different clustering decisions should be explorable through the second version of the model browser.]

Explicating Prophetic Texts

For early Seventh-day Adventist authors, the Biblical books of Daniel and Revelations offered the keys for situating themselves and their readers in time. Informed by their “rationalist” approach to the Bible, whereby they hold that all of the Bible has a clear meaning that can be understood by the faithful reader, they approach the Bible as a guidebook with clear if coded information.25 Building on a Protestant understanding of history as the linear unfolding of a divine plan that stretches from creation to the second coming, the early Seventh-day Adventists sought to identify their current position in that progression, leading up to their final salvation at Jesus’ second coming. To do so, they looked particularly to the book of Daniel to explain events of the past and to the book of Revelations to explain current events and anticipate the events to come. In these books, part of the Apocalyptic literature of the Bible, the authors look forward in time and tell of the overthrow of world powers and the eventual establishment of God’s kingdom.26 Containing visions populated with fantastical symbolic creatures, from a leopard with four wings and four heads to beasts and dragons, the authors used coded language to encourage their audience with hope of the coming fall of oppressive powers and coming days of peace.27

Seventh-day Adventist authors derived their understanding of how to interpret these text and what they represented from William Miller. Born into a religious Baptist family, Miller embraced deism in his twenties, but found himself religiously unsettled by his experiences during the War of 1812. Returning to the Baptist church, he experienced a religious conversion marked by being overwhelmed by emotions and feeling the truth and value of the Baptist narrative of salvation.28 With a faith grounded in a conversion experience, Miller turned his attention to understanding and articulating the reasonableness of that faith. Working from a set of fourteen rules, which he derived from Biblical proof texts, he developed an interpretation of the Bible, and particularly the prophetic texts, that resolved its apparent contradictions – thereby satisfying the critiques of his deist friends – and that also revealed the approximate date of the looked-for second coming: 1843.29

Charts, such as the one to the left, were used by Millerite preachers to explain to audiences how to interpret the prophecies in Daniel and Revelations. Part of the publishing and outreach efforts of Joshua V. Himes, the charts provided a visual representation of Miller’s complicated, but methodical, interpretive work. In the upper left corner, the images from Daniel are depicted and aligned to show their correlation, with the head of the statue of Daniel, chapter 2, aligned with the lion of Daniel, chapter 7, the silver chest and arms of chapter 2 with the bear of chapter 7 and the ram of chapter 8 and so forth. Across the middle, the chart bridges between the books and Daniel and Revelations through the depictions of “Pagan Rome” - the iron legs of the statue in Daniel 2, the beast of Daniel 7, and the dragon of Revelations 12. The bottom half of the chart correlates the events of history since Jesus’ death with the extended images of Revelations. All of these different elements are tied together through the dates and computations that associate the years of different historical events with the periods of time recorded in the prophetic texts.

Early Seventh-day Adventists reconciled the continuation of time after 1844 with Miller’s interpretations by arguing that Miller’s interpretation as basically correct, but that they had misunderstood the significance of October 22, 1844. While most Millerites either concluded that the dates had been miscalculated or that Miller’s whole enterprise had been misguided, a small group embraced an interpretation put forward by Hiram Edson that the “cleansing of the sanctuary” referred not to the earth as Miller had thought but marked “a new phase of Christ’s ministry in heaven that placed the earth under judgment.”30 How long this new phase would last was unknown, but believers could point to the fulfilled prophecies to know that they were indeed living in the last days.

As a result, the interpretation of Daniel and Revelations found in Millerite charts continued to play a central role to Seventh-day Adventist efforts to situate themselves temporally. Captured across three topics of the topic model, Seventh-day Adventist authors used the figures and dates of Daniel and Revelations throughout their writings to argue for their unique sense of time, to explain current events, and to anticipate events to come.

As indicated in the above charts, while descriptions of prophetic texts and the work of situating readers within the Seventh-day Adventist temporal imaginary has a continual presence within the periodical literature of the denomination, its prevalence relative to other concerns decreased over time. This is the case even when looking only at the central denominational titles, excluding the topical and regional titles that proliferated after the 1880s. This is not to say that SDA authors became less interested in or came to question the uses of these texts over time or the temporal imaginary they were used to construct. Full explications of the texts and republication of material from the 1850s can be seen well into the 20th century.31 The decline is better understood as reflecting the embrace of the SDA system for explicating the texts of Daniel and Revelations and the development of a consensus around the position of the Adventist people in sacred time. While later authors may remind their readers of the standard interpretations, they were building on existing beliefs, rather than striving to convince their readers of a new sense of time, and so required less discursive space to communicate their message.

Eschatology - Describing the Second Coming

With their roots in the belief that 1844 marked the beginning of the final events before the second coming, eschatology, or the theological study of “last things,” has a significant presence in SDA literature and in their temporal orientation. From Ellen White’s seminal work, The Great Controversy, to some of their most distinctive theological contributions, including the Sanctuary Doctrine, Conditional Immortality, and the Sabbath Doctrine (discussed in Chapter One), understanding and describing the world to come and the events leading up to it was the focus of much of the intellectual energy of the early Seventh-day Adventists.32 While most Christian groups anticipate Jesus’ return in some form, for Seventh-day Adventists that return is central to their distinctive understanding of Scripture and their self-understanding as God’s chosen people.

The topics I identified as relating to eschatology, or the study of end-times, fit into two general categories. The first set of topics, including #170, #182, and #199 offer descriptions of heaven and the experience of the second coming, using biblical passages and poetry to remind believers of the goal of the Adventist Christian life and warnings about anticipated hardships leading up to the second coming. The second set, which includes #51, #117, and #145, outlines some of the unique theological positions the denomination took with regard to the requirements for salvation. These topics remind readers of what to expect in the days leading up to the second coming. They also provide justifications as to why events did not unfold as previously expected, using the concept of progressive revelation, or “Present Truth,” to emphasize that God reveals his plan gradually and through imperfect messengers.33

While the trajectory of these topics shows a slow decline over time in their prominence in the denominational literature, this again does not mean that these topics disappear from the denominational literature. During the first few decades of the denomination, these topics were key to establishing what would become standard Seventh-day Adventist understandings of the soul, the work of salvation, and the role of Adventists in the final events before the second coming. As these concepts became more ingrained in Adventist theology and became basic to their cultural imaginary, fewer words would have been needed to invoke these ideas for readers.

Interpreting the Signs of the Times

As a people eagerly awaiting the second coming and who believed that they could orient themselves in divine time by matching current events with events described in the Bible, denominational members closely watched news and world events. From cataloging catastrophic events and examples of government oversteps in regulating religious behavior to extended analyses of world events in light of prophecy, nearly every world event held the potential of signaling some new phase in the events leading up to the second coming. While commentators often warned readers against setting dates and reminded them that their knowledge was incomplete, the regularity of the topics served to remind readers that they were indeed living in the last days. As such, they were called on to make themselves ready and to share the Adventist message with the world.

The signs frequently mentioned by Adventist commentators range from concerns over sin and social ills to commentary on world events in light of prophecy. Spiritualism, then a prominent competitor in the religious space, and sin “as in the days of Noah” were of particular concern in the early years of the denomination (topics #26, #86). In later years, as the attention of the denomination shifted outwards, concerns about war and social unrest (topics #27, #39, #141, #163) were the primary markers of the current point in divine time. At the turn of the century, the growing influence of Progressive reformers and those advocating for Sunday observance laws loomed particularly large in the Adventist imaginary, as signs that the anticipated collusion between the United States and the Catholic Church to enforce Sunday worship and persecute Adventists was at hand (topics #158, #242). Among the more curious “signs” are those recorded in topic #100, which captures frequent retellings of the darkening of the sun on May 19, 1780 and accounts of stars falling on November 13, 1833, some of the more supernatural-seeming events portending the second coming.34 And throughout the period, authors warned readers to anticipate unrest and persecution in the time leading up to the Jesus’ return (topic #179). World events were not just curiosities, but vital clues in tracing the unfolding of God’s plan.

Threats to the Separation of Church and State

One particular topic of concerns, and one that developed as Seventh-day Adventist began focusing more on the role of United States in the events leading up to the second coming, was the threat of the legal establishment of religion. This was a particular concern for early Seventh-day Adventists, as they had identified the first amendment and the prohibition against the establishment of religion as key aspects of the uniqueness of the United States, and the establishment of religion as the first step in the unfolding of the persecution of Adventists prior to the second coming. As resistance to the legislation of religion was understood to be one of the marks of true believers, believers tracked efforts to promote the passing of religion laws, and politically organized members to resist those efforts.

During this period of study, the most prominent movements to legislate behavior and religious practice occurred during the closing decades of the nineteenth century. Often in connection with temperance movements, Protestant religious leaders promoted what they claimed to be laws promoting general morality and social norms regarding Sunday observance. While at times these laws were drafted granting exceptions for those who designated other days for religious worship, Seventh-day Adventist leaders and others decried them as attacks on freedom of religion and the principle of religious liberty. Any attempt to exercise state power in issues of religion was the beginning of the end, both of the nation and of time, for Adventist commentators.

So important was this issue to the Adventist readership that it received a series dedicated periodical titles - Liberty, Sentinel of Liberty. In looking at the overall prevalence of the topic, these individual titles exaggerate the prevalence of the topic particularly in the years surrounding 1890. However, even when looking just at these topics in the central denominational titles, an increase in attention is visible, first around 1890 and again around 1905, in concerns about church and state.

Tracing Periods of Expectation

Examining the prevalence of all of these topics across the first seventy years of the denomination, two general features emerge. First, over time the prevalence of these topics decreases, as denominational members settle into the realization that the work of redemption was going to require much more time than had been anticipated by early church leaders in 1850. The reflects on the one hand a “naturalizing” of the discourses of end times, as the understanding of end times events and the role of the Seventh-day Adventist people in preparing for Jesus’ second coming entered into the realm of the “known” or the imaginary of the denomination. On the other hand, the decline also reflects a lengthening of the temporal imaginary, as the work facing denomination members - to reach the world with the third angel’s message - was a large undertaking that would require both time and significant effort on the part of members. [I think I have something from Bull here about how, with the death of EGW, the denomination settled in for the long haul (and turned more conservative).]

While the overall trajectory is one of decline, charting the prevalence of end-times topics also suggests four general periods of end-times expectation and readjustment over the first 70 years of the denominations history. The first, and the clearest, wave of expectation stretches from the start of the Seventh-day Adventist publishing endeavors in 1849 and reaches until approximately 1858. The second series of spikes starts around 1868 and reaches about 1875. The third, seen both across all titles and just the denominational titles, stretches from around 1886 to 1898. And the final period of unrest appears at the end of this study, starting around 1910.

This pattern fits with, while also expands, the secondary literature on the development of the denomination. In Seeking a Sanctuary, authors Bull and Lockhart note that the Seventh-day Adventist community has historically tended to be relatively quiet about end-times during periods of disruption, such as war, while instead active in periods prior or following.35 This pattern matches that captured by the topic model, as periods of heightened discourse occur in the years following the civil war, and the years leading up to the first World War. While the authors note this pattern as a curiosity, the pattern makes sense given the particular attention to the union of church and state power as the key marker of the start of the final days, and their self-understanding as the faithful remnant who would be persecuted at the end. Periods of war and conflict, while distressing and a sign of things to come, were not conducive to the type of global unification and establishment of religion that would mark the final confrontation.

Adventist theologian Jon Paulien has identified over twenty attempts to predict the date of the second coming over the history of Seventh-day Adventism, from 1844 to the 1990. Among these were repeated predictions between 1844 and 1851, a series of predictions between 1884 and 1894, and again in light of the events of World War I. While he notes that Ellen White herself repeatedly discouraged the setting of dates, for a significant percentage of believers, during these periods word events and biblical interpretation seemed to line up in such a way to suggest that the time was at hand.36 These peaks in Adventist attempts to name the date of the second coming again matches the general pattern of the model, with the model showing an additional spike in the years around 1870. This corroboration between the secondary literature and the model suggests that the model is indeed capturing and coherently classifying the linguistic features of the denominations periodical literature and that the topics I have isolated are productively showing those trends.

A Community of Belief

The primary goal for Ellen and James White in the first six years their publishing work was to unite the Seventh-day Adventist community around the belief in the Sabbath, and the law more broadly, as the key that explained Jesus’ delay since 1844 and provided the mark that distinguished true believers.

Around 1855, having established their common foundation in Saturday worship and still awaiting the second coming, the denominational literature began to shift toward a focus on the lived religious experience of these early members, both in the form encouragement of spiritual growth and in the sharing of stories through the writing and publication of personal testimonials.

1849-1855 focus on early rhetoric most intense period of expectation, unsurprisingly as it is coming right after Miller and as they are focused on a new belief (Sabbath) as the test for salvation.

gender here: - ellen white’s visions are held as authoritative - publication in periodical declines for a time (part of effort to establish credibility) - gender of early corresponders seems to be of little significance - while men and women were likely to write about different things, both were published. Often women were particularly celebrated as examples of faith in the face of resistence from friends/family - theology was a largely masculine endeavor, but the visions of EGW served as the final “stamp” of their approval.

A Community of Practice

By the mid 1860s, the emphases within the denomination shifted again, this time to practices that further distinguished Seventh-day Adventists from their Protestant neighbors. In 186?, Ellen White recorded her first visions on the topic of health, expanding the emphasis on the natural law that informed SDA organizations of time to the physical health of bodies.

The growing emphasis on health marks

Whereas during the early years of the denomination, very little was published about gender and the relative roles of men and women within the church, the growing emphasis on religious practices, particularly in relation to health and diet, brought issues of gender into the forefront of the denominational discourse.

The growing emphasis on domesticity has instructive ties to broader nineteenth-century shifts in conceptions of gender and its relationship to religion.

Within Seventh-day Adventism, while the domestic space was increasingly stressed as the linchpin in the development (and salvation) of children and the overall spiritual health of the whole families, the vision of gender roles was closer to those ascribed to pre-nineteenth-century New England than those common to the nineteenth century.

Here conceptions of time are useful for explaining why early Seventh-day Adventists seemed somewhat immune to the surrounding shifts in conceptions of gender. Whereas their Protestant neighbors increasingly embraced notions of progress and upward (individual) mobility as the underlying narrative, Seventh-day Adventism, with their emphasis on the approaching second coming and general skepticism toward the state, provided a different standard against which both men and women measured success and negotiated their respective roles.

A Community of Action

By the end of the nineteenth century, the focus of denominational leaders shifted outward toward missionary efforts and toward political concerns.

Missions for early SDA took many forms, not just preaching but distribution of tracts and periodical literature and involvement in health care.

While preaching was a predominantly male activity in early SDA (EGW excepted), working as a colporteur or in health care were venues open to and encouraged for members of both sexes.

[anecdote to start]

In this dissertation, I examine the unique religious culture that developed during the first eighty years of Seventh-day Adventism. I argue that cycles of end-times expectation and the religious leadership of Ellen White contributed to the formation of a religious culture marked by domestic authority, cooperative organization, and the activism of women, seen in the movement’s religious understanding and pursuit of health. This culture provides an instructive counterpoint to accounts of nineteenth-century revivalism that stress the reinforcement of patriarchal structures and capitalistic economic structures in the aftermath of the revivals of the nineteenth century.

Women and the Revivals of the Early Republic

As will be discussed in the first essay, the early nineteenth-century was a period in American history marked by religious innovation. The separation of religion from state control, a process known as disestablishment, created an environment particularly ripe for a “democratization” of religious expression.1 People were increasingly able to worship according to their preference and to establish churches outside of the control of the Anglican (Episcopal) church in the South and the Congregational church in New England. As a result of disestablishment, the Baptist and Methodist traditions, which had existed both in the colonies and in Britain and Europe prior to the Revolution, flourished in the American context. Membership in Methodist churches grew to 250,000 by 1820 and 500,000 by 1830, nearly four percent of the population, and Baptists saw a similar increase, with membership growing “tenfold” in the decades after the Revolution.2 The loosening of social controls on religious expression also resulted in increasing diversity among religious traditions, as new churches, denominations, and movements formed in response to differences in religious thought and practice. Out of this period of religious innovation came some of the most distinctive American religious and social movements, including the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, the Oneida Utopian Community, and the Seventh-day Adventists.3

The decentralization of control, however, is not sufficient to explain the rapid proliferation of new religious movements, each claiming to present the truth that others were failing uphold or communicate. Looking more closely at religious revival and reform movements, it becomes clear that these religious actors were guided by particular visions of sacred history, by particular understandings of the arc of history and the role of American Protestant Christians in that narrative. While each group understood itself as standing at the crux of the story of salvation, all shared a framework that “began in Eden, developed in the world, and would culminate in a world without end.” The narrative was radically expansive, encompassing “humankind – saints and sinners, men and women, common and chosen …” along with “the suprahuman character of God Himself, His son the Christ, and the sworn enemy – the Antichrist.”4 In the march toward the last judgment, each group identified itself as the chosen one whose members successfully understood and obeyed the requirements for salvation, whether those requirements were correct behavior, correct attitude toward the divine, or the proper experience to ensure a connection with and the favor of the Divine. For many, and particularly for those traditions coming out of New England Puritanism, that position also required bringing about change in the world, either by converting souls through revival or by advocating for virtuous living. These various Protestant groups saw themselves as having a divine mission to prepare the world for the coming end and to do their part to ensure that events unfolded according to the Divine plan.

Protestant women as well as men embraced these various efforts to redeem the world ahead of the imminent return of Christ. As has been noted by Ann Braude and others, religion in the American context has always been a site of significant female activity.5 Although leadership positions have been restricted to male adherents across most of the American religious traditions, women have consistently constituted the majority of those who attend, who contribute both time and money to religious initiatives, and who work to train children within the religious tradition.6 Building on the existing predominance of religious women, the Protestant reform movements of the early nineteenth-century called upon women to help bring about revival and reform. As Carroll Smith-Rosenberg has noted, although these movements were generally led by “male clerics and reformers … women were their most zealous adherents.”7 In addition to joining radical religious movements, women worked for reform in a variety of ways, from fundraising for various causes to creating female benevolent societies to themselves taking to the pulpit and preaching to convince others to repent for the kingdom of heaven was at hand. Through all these efforts, women created “a public and powerful role for themselves as a female conscience and moral voice crying in a wilderness of male corruption” during the same period that domesticity and “the Cult of True Womanhood” grew in cultural prominence.8

Radical religious movements attracted the involvement of women and presented new opportunities for them to claim leadership roles that had been previously been denied. Sociologists and historians have linked periods of revival and radical religion to periods of social and economic change and distress, when “boundaries are no longer clearly defined.”9 Revivals, as “liminal” periods, provided space for the reconfiguration of social norms and structures, enabling women and others traditionally excluded from leadership roles to experiment with different constructions and in so doing, shift the shape of the social spheres.10 For the revivals of the Second Great Awakening, the social reorganization launched with the American Revolution and the instability of society brought about with increased mobility and the loosening of government control on the expression of religion created the environment in which groups traditional excluded - those without formal training in divinity, women, and ethnic minorities - could experiment with alternative structures of religious practice and qualification.

For the women drawn to radical religion, their involvement took a variety of forms, from active preaching to more gender-conforming support roles, and was explained in a variety of ways. While preaching and teaching in front of mix gender groups constituted in many ways the height of women’s break from the cultural norms, there were additional avenues open to those who did not directly feel the call to preach. From working within the growing outreach organizations of the revival movements as “social workers, teachers, managers, missionaries, and writers” to encouraging revivals “through home meeting, prayer groups, and voluntary and missions work,” women found a range of opportunities where they could contribute to the cause.11 The “social” space of religious life, positioned as it was between the “public” and “private,” between commerce or government and the family, provided a range of opportunities for women to apply their faith.12 In defending their assumption of more forward roles in the promotion of the faith, religious women deployed a variety of strategies to navigate the balance between their religious convictions and the religious and cultural constraints. For some, and particularly for adventists, Scripture itself could be invoked for support, especially Joel’s prophecy that in the last days God’s spirit would be poured out on both young men and women. As a result, “the sight of a woman standing in the pulpit had cosmic significance: she was a living symbol of the last days.”13 For others, they relied on what became a standard set of strategies for situating themselves and their calling within an acceptable religious framework. Nearly all in telling their stories inform their audience of their strong resistance to the call, and often of their attempts to avoid it. Eventually, however, they find that they cannot resist, and so appeal to the listeners sympathy in claiming that “the authority of God outweighs that of … parents, husbands, and friend, even that of their own conscience.”14 By separating their activity from “ambition” or personal desire, and presenting themselves as weak and (apparently) unwilling vessels, women within revival movements were able to find an unstable ground on which to claim some authority within revival movements.

[Briefly, Millerites.]

Ellen and James White and the Pioneers of Seventh-day Adventism

The three central figures of early Seventh-day Adventism were the husband and wife pair of James and Ellen White, and Joseph Bates.

Additionally, the histories of Seventh-day Day Adventism include nine other men (and their less-often mentioned wives) as the pioneers of the denomination. These were … Together, this group of (initially) young men worked together to edit the newspapers of the denomination, to debate and determine the theology of the denomination, and to spread the word as the primary missionaries.

While not granted the status of a “pioneer” of the denomination, one additional figure who significantly shaped their approach to health as part of religious practices was John Harvey Kellogg.

Building a Computational Study of Religious Culture

[why using computational methods for this study. Framework within which those methods are deployed.]

Early Seventh-day Adventists, like their predecessors in the Millerite and Christian Connection movements, were highly prolific writers, relying on print publications to spread their message and win converts. As a result, even within just the periodical literature of the denomination, there is more written content than can be effectively managed for historical analysis. As a result, previous studies of Seventh-day Adventism have relied primarily on the major publication of the denomination, The Review and Herald, or relied on selective reading to explore different aspects or periods of the denomination’s history.

The development of computational methods for classifying texts offers a third way to approach the prolific periodical literature of the denomination.

Reading Religious Culture through Topic Models

[methodology section on using topic modeling]

The Structure of A Gospel of Health and Salvation

Works of historical scholarship typically take a narrative format, telling the story of the past and showing how various cultural forces and human actors shaped the development of historical events. However, the development of computational technologies creates the space and the need to also consider the processes by which historical interpretation takes place. While this dissertation includes elements of historical story-telling, my primary focus is on methodology, specifically, the incorporation of computational models of text into the work of historical analysis. As such, this dissertation is an applied methodological study organized around a historical research question: how does time, and the expectation of the second coming, shape the development of the religious culture of Seventh-day Adventism?

At the core of the project is the browser of the topic model of the SDA literature, accessible at http://browser.dissertation.jeriwieringa.com. This model, built using MALLET and visualized using Andrew Goldstone’s DfR Browser, provides a window onto the language used across the corpus of Seventh-day Adventist texts that I assembled. The interface is organized according to my interpretation of those topics, as reflected in the topic labels. I discuss my interpretive process for creating the labels in chapter two.

The work of selecting and preparing a corpus of text for topic modeling is one of interpretation, and sets the limits of possibility for the resulting computational model. As Supporting the model are the dissertation notebooks, which document the technical work that went into creating and interpreting the topic model.

The first essay, “The Emergence of Seventh-day Adventism,” provides an overview of Seventh-day Adventism in light of nineteenth-century religion and culture. This chapter is aimed at the reader who is unfamiliar with the context of American religious history or the particulars of the SDA, providing the necessary context for the interpretations forwarded throughout the rest of the dissertation.

The second essay, “Constructing Computational Models from Historical Texts,” provides methodological statements for the sources, processing, modeling, and interpretive aspects of the project. This chapter is the most technical in content, while also providing the framing links tying the computational work to the historical interpretation.

The third chapter, “Anticipating the End of Time,” establishes the problem of time within early Seventh-day Adventism and uses the topic model to identify four major cycles of end-times expectation during the first seventy years of the denomination’s history. A case study on using topic models to identify and reveal overarching trends in a corpus for historical analysis, the chapter Tracing the prominence of end-times related topics throughout the periodical literature of the denomination, the chapter bridges the computational model and more traditional historical research into the development of the particular religious culture of Seventh-day Adventism.

The forth and final chapter, “,” offers a second case study for the use of topic modeling and textual analysis for historical research, this time at the level of close reading. Where chapter 3 focused on broad patterns, chapter four explore in detail the gender dynamics in two prominent areas of Christian labor: home and missions.

As a project based on the computational analysis of text, a large portion of the intellectual and scholarly work the make up the dissertation exists in code. In considering the methodological processes around the use of computational analysis in history, this dissertation makes the claim, both explicitly and implicitly, that this “technical” work is of central importance to the scholarly object of the dissertation. Where traditional methods of review rely on the use of clear and well formatted footnotes so that the trail of evidence can be retraced and evaluated, the review of computational driven work requires the use of documented and accessible code, so that both the execution of the techniques and the assumptions embedded within the technical choices, can be seen and evaluated. The code elements can be viewed through the dissertation’s web interface, or can be downloaded and run either for verification or for adaptation to other projects. The work of making the technical elements of the dissertation visible and extensible is key to establishing processes for validating computationally-based scholarship in the humanities, an extension of the push for reproducible research in the sciences.

The final elements of the dissertation provide documentation for the different components of the projects, including the final website, the model browser, and the dissertation sources. Per the requirements of the Department of History and Art History at George Mason University, the project includes a process statement, which provides an account of the methods and technologies used in the creation of the dissertation. Traditional documentation elements, such as bibliography and acknowledgments, are also included in the “About” section. Together, all of these aspects of the project constitute the body of work that is A Gospel of Health and Salvation.

While the dissertation itself is the composite of these different computational and interpretive elements, readers do not need to be experts in all aspects of the project in order to read and evaluate the dissertation. The essays outline my approach and my intellectual decision in structuring and carrying out the computational analysis, providing an overview of the work without requiring the reader to directly engage the computational aspects of the work. Including the code enables readers to evaluate how well I have implemented those ideas and are included as part of a commitment to reproducible research. The concept of reproducible research, while increasingly prevalent in the sciences, is less common in the humanities. It refers to the goal of sufficiently describing ones computational methods and process so that others can reproduce the results when given the same data.15 Although the emphasis on code and computation is new, the concept of making historical research verifiable is not, as historians have long incorporated methods for verification in their academic writing through the mechanism of footnotes.16 By releasing the code and describing the processes used, scholars who rely on computational methods provide the information necessary for that work to be recognized and critically engaged, and in so doing make it part of the scholarly conversation.

item.title: The Emergence of Seventh-day Adventism
item.dc:creator: Jeri E. Wieringa
